articles.content: S&P 500 forecast after the AI bubble panic: Why Friday's selloff is not yet a major bearish reversal Friday's selloff in AI and chip stocks looked alarming, but the S&P 500 E-mini futures (ES) are telling a somewhat less frightening story. Following the October 16 close, my four-hour technical analysis still shows a decline within a broader trading range, rather than a confirmed major bearish trend reversal. The next important test is around 7,668, and I explain why in my video below: AI stocks were hit hard, but the broader market tells a different story For investors holding semiconductor and AI-related stocks, Friday was certainly an uncomfortable day. As Adam Button reported in AI names fall as the Nasdaq comes under fresh pressure, selling extended beyond chipmakers into AI infrastructure, cloud computing and cybersecurity companies. Some individual stocks suffered much steeper losses than the broader equity indices. The investingLive Americas market wrap showed the Nasdaq down approximately 2.3% on Friday, compared with a 1.2% decline in the S&P 500. That difference is worth paying attention to. A sharp decline in popular technology stocks can create the impression that the entire stock market is entering a major collapse. However, weakness in market leaders does not necessarily mean that the broader market has already confirmed a bearish reversal. We also saw a different picture internationally. European stocks finished higher on Friday and posted weekly gains, illustrating how unevenly the selling pressure was distributed. This does not make the risks in AI stocks disappear. It simply suggests that we should distinguish between a sharp sector selloff and a confirmed breakdown in the broader stock market. And that brings me to the S&P 500 chart. Watch my S&P 500 futures technical analysis and forecast in the video below. I explain the trading range, the price channel and the conditions that would make me considerably more bearish. Why the S&P 500 still looks like a trading range The central observation in my analysis is that ES remains within a recognizable trading range. On the four-hour chart, price has been moving through alternating advances and declines, with sellers taking control near resistance and buyers responding around support. I also identify a price channel that has helped frame these movements since September. The channel's boundaries and midpoint have repeatedly interacted with price, including around the latest decline. In particular, the recent selling followed a rejection near two overlapping resistance references: the channel's midpoint and the upper boundary of the range's value area. The value area is the price region where roughly 70% of the trading volume occurred over the period being examined. Its upper and lower boundaries can help identify where the market has previously accepted substantial trading activity. After failing near resistance, ES moved back toward the lower boundary of that value area. This brings us to an especially interesting part of Friday's price action. S&P 500 futures: Why 7,668 matters Around 7,668, several technical references come together. First, this is approximately the lower boundary of the value area for the range examined in the video. Second, the October 16 decline approached the lower boundary of the price channel. Third, the market was revisiting a support region associated with earlier lows around September 18 and October 1. These are three different reasons why traders might pay attention to approximately the same area. For example, some short sellers may decide to take profits when price reaches established support. Other traders may consider a speculative long position, while traders following the channel could view the lower boundary as an area where a rebound becomes possible. I am not claiming to know which participants were buying or covering shorts on Friday. The observation is that price reached an area where several recognizable support references converged. The important point is that Friday's decline had not yet produced the sustained breakdown below this area that I would want to see before interpreting the move as a more significant bearish development. That does not mean support must hold on the next test. It means the market has not yet provided sufficient evidence for my more bearish scenario. What would turn the S&P 500 outlook more bearish? This is where my forecast becomes conditional. In my opinion, the more meaningful warning would be two or three consecutive completed four-hour candles closing below approximately 7,668. Why not simply react to the first move below that level? Because markets frequently cross support or resistance briefly before reversing direction. A momentary break can reflect a liquidity event or a failed attempt to establish a new trading range. Several consecutive closes below support would provide stronger evidence that sellers are establishing acceptance at lower prices, rather than merely pushing the market temporarily beyond a familiar boundary. An additional development worth watching would be a subsequent recovery attempt that fails to reclaim the broken support. For example, if ES breaks below 7,668, rebounds toward that area, encounters renewed selling and then continues lower, the bearish interpretation becomes more credible. Even then, a downside break would not automatically establish a long-term bear market. It would first signal that the current trading range is potentially resolving lower, with the wider trend requiring further evaluation. And what if S&P 500 support holds? The alternative is that buyers continue defending the existing support region. If ES holds around 7,668 and begins recovering, the next question becomes whether price can reclaim the channel's midpoint and challenge the higher-volume resistance region that previously attracted selling. Such a recovery would fit the existing trading-range interpretation. However, I would be careful about declaring a new bullish breakout simply because the market rebounds from support. There is an important difference between a recovery within a range and a sustained move out of that range. A rebound could improve the immediate technical picture while leaving the broader market in consolidation. For now, I am not automatically bullish or bearish. My interpretation is that the recent weakness is meaningful, but the evidence for a major bearish reversal remains incomplete. The next catalysts: Technology earnings, inflation and the Federal Reserve Technical support is only part of the picture. Investors also need to consider what could change market sentiment as trading resumes. The upcoming earnings calendar could be particularly important for determining whether AI-related selling remains concentrated in certain stocks or spreads further across the market. As discussed in Earnings week ahead: Banks were upbeat on the economy, now onto tech, the latest bank results suggested that important parts of the US economy remain resilient. The next earnings announcements will provide another opportunity to evaluate how businesses are navigating current conditions. Meanwhile, inflation, energy prices and monetary policy remain potential sources of volatility. Giuseppe Dellamotta's review of changing interest-rate expectations illustrates how traders are reassessing the Federal Reserve outlook amid persistent inflation concerns. One reason this matters for stocks is that higher costs do not necessarily translate into higher corporate profits. Justin Low offers a useful explanation in Why higher inflation doesn't always mean bigger corporate profits. These macroeconomic concerns also formed part of my earlier Dow Jones futures analysis for October 16, although that analysis reflected an earlier market snapshot before Friday's selling intensified. Taken together, the question for the coming week is whether disappointing developments cause the broader indices to break established support, or whether the latest weakness remains largely a correction within existing trading structures. My S&P 500 forecast: Respect the selling, but wait for confirmation My main takeaway after reviewing Friday's price action is straightforward. The selling pressure is real, particularly in technology stocks, but the S&P 500 futures chart is not yet confirming the kind of major bearish trend reversal that some investors may fear. The market has reached an important support region, and the next reaction around 7,668 could provide useful information. Holding that region would keep the existing trading-range interpretation intact. Sustained four-hour closes below it, particularly followed by a failed recovery, would make me reassess the bearish risks more seriously. The market could certainly move lower. I am not ruling that out. But there is a difference between anticipating a major reversal and having sufficient evidence that one is actually developing. For traders and investors, recognizing that difference can help avoid making decisions based purely on frightening headlines or the latest sharp move in a few popular stocks. S&P 500 forecast on a wider perspective (the simple weekly chart) I typically perform some heavy and sophisticated analysis with lots of data but for traders and investors at investingLive.com, I like to simplify and show them the simple charts. Less is more for many of our readers. That is where apx 7600 (shown as 7,608.89 below) comes in, if S&P 500 decides to sell some more. S&P 500 futures: The weekly 20 EMA in my above simple chart could become an important support test S&P 500 E-mini futures (ES) remain in a broader uptrend on the weekly chart, although the latest pullback suggests buyers are facing renewed pressure near the highs. During the week ending October 16, futures approached the previous week's high near 7,900, but failed to extend the rally. The contract subsequently declined to close around 7,703, a weekly loss of approximately 2.1%. Despite this weakness, the broader bullish structure has not yet been decisively undermined. The first area to watch is around 7,670-7,680. The latest weekly low near 7,676 almost matched the late-September low around 7,673, making this an immediate reference area for potential stabilization. Further below, the 20-week exponential moving average (EMA), currently around 7,609, could become an important support reference if the decline continues. This moving average has been rising alongside the broader advance. However, price has not yet tested it during the latest pullback, so its ability to attract renewed buying interest remains unproven. A decline toward the EMA followed by a convincing weekly rebound would support the interpretation that the market is experiencing a correction within a continuing uptrend. Conversely, a completed weekly close below the moving average, followed by an unsuccessful attempt to recover it, would suggest that the correction may be developing into something more significant. The early-September lows around 7,575-7,585 provide another nearby structural reference. On the upside, a sustained recovery toward 7,850-7,900 would help restore the bullish case. The takeaway: The weekly 20 EMA offers a potentially useful future support test, but the more important evidence will be how prices behave if they reach it. A moving average identifies an area worth watching, not a guarantee that buyers will defend it. This analysis reflects the October 16, 2026 market close and is my technical interpretation as of October 17. It is educational commentary, not financial advice. This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Stochastic SEIR dynamics via graph Laplacian diffusion under transmission uncertainty
articles.desc: Epidemic spatial spread across interconnected populations depends on both mobility between locations and random fluctuations in transmission. We extend the Susceptible-Exposed-Infected-Removed (SEIR) epidemic model to a network setting by introducing graph Laplacian diffusion to capture population m
articles.content: Epidemic spatial spread across interconnected populations depends on both mobility between locations and random fluctuations in transmission. We extend the Susceptible-Exposed-Infected-Removed (SEIR) epidemic model to a network setting by introducing graph Laplacian diffusion to capture population mobility, and further incorporate stochastic perturbations in the transmission rate to capture environmental noise. Using Lyapunov function analysis, we first establish that the stochastic system admits a unique global solution which remains non-negative for all time, so that the model is mathematically well-posed and its state variables retain their epidemiological meaning as population counts. Building on this well-posedness, we then apply Lyapunov techniques a second time to analyse the long-term behaviour of the solution. The disease-free equilibrium is shown to be globally asymptotically stable when the basic reproduction number does not exceed one, indicating disease extinction. When the basic reproduction number exceeds one, the disease instead persists, in the sense that the stochastic solution exhibits a bounded time-averaged deviation from the endemic equilibrium of the corresponding deterministic system. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods are further employed for parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification, applied to COVID-19 incidence data across all 47 prefectures in Japan. The proposed framework brings together network-driven mobility, stochastic transmission dynamics, and Bayesian uncertainty quantification within a SEIR model. Finally, computational experiments on a small-world Watts-Strogatz network are used to validate and visually illustrate the theoretical results.

articles.title: Opinion: Herald-Republic pushes for human answers in local political races
articles.desc: As use of Artificial Intelligence becomes pervasive, it should be no surprise local candidates are using it as part of their campaigns.
articles.content: Opinion: Herald-Republic pushes for human answers in local political races | Elections | yakimaherald.com You have permission to edit this article. Santa is coming to town! Watch as NORAD tracks Santa live on yakimaherald.com. Envelopes from processed ballots sit in bins at the Yakima County Courthouse Tuesday, Nov. 6, 2024, in Yakima, Wash. As use of Artificial Intelligence becomes pervasive, it should be no surprise local candidates are using it as part of their campaigns. Our reporters traditionally reach out to candidates with questions in the weeks before the election. Depending on the race, some of these interviews happen in person or by phone. In other races, we use written questionnaires sent by email. We relied on in-person and phone interviews for the stories we’ve run about the 4th District congressional race, the sheriff’s candidates, auditor and the two 14th District House races. We sent questionnaires to candidates for state House in the 15th District, treasurer and assessor. As part of the editing process, we ran the written responses through Pangram, an AI detection tool. Pangram found the responses from Reedy Berg, Sam Johnson and Chris Corry were AI-generated. Since we didn’t tell the candidates in advance not to use AI, we gave them two options — an interview in person or by phone, or to let readers know they were using AI for their responses. Corry and Johnson agreed to interviews, and were happy to talk about how they were using AI in their campaigns. Berg said he would “humanize” his responses in an email, but didn’t get back to us by our print deadline. We tried several times to contact him by phone and email. To meet our deadline, we used his AI answers with labeling. as text that was produced primarily by an AI model with little human editing. Corry said he put his beliefs, values and guiding principles in an AI prompt, then edited responses for accuracy and to ensure they matched his voice. Johnson used it in a similar manner. Using AI isn’t unusual in local political races these days, and candidates are using AI for questionnaire responses elsewhere in the state. RANGE, a news organization in Spokane, ran candidate responses it received through AI-detection programs and found multiple candidates . RANGE also found a large number of op-eds at Spokane publications implemented a “no AI” rule for its op-eds this week. We don’t allow our reporters or editors to write using AI at the Herald-Republic, and we don’t want candidates to use it in the Herald-Republic without telling you. Our reporters use AI assistance with transcription (with a human check), spelling, grammar and for research (with human verification). We don’t use AI to generate our stories. We owe it to our readers to be transparent about what we are sharing and how. We understand that candidates are bombarded with questions and requests in the final weeks before the election, and AI can help campaigns respond to and process all those requests. We also know that things are changing fast and the conversation might be different next year. We do everything we can to encourage candidates to share their thoughts with our readers. In recent years, we’ve had more candidates skip our questions or not respond at all. That can be telling — if candidates aren’t answering questions from the newspaper or submitting information for the voter guide, how will they respond to their constituents once they are elected? We’ve found most candidates for the general election this year were responsive and willing to talk to us. The Herald-Republic is working to update its op-ed policy and its election coverage guide to be clear about use of AI. We’re interested in what you think. Send us a letter to the editor by emailing . If you’d like to share your thoughts about AI with us but don’t want them published, email Joanna Markell is the managing editor of the Yakima Herald-Republic. articles.desc: Understand the speeds your Ethernet cable can transmit at help you diagnose where the slowdowns on your network are happening.
articles.content: How To Check Your Ethernet Cable's Speed (And Not Your Home Network's) That 100 Mbps result doesn't automatically mean your Ethernet cable is bad. Here's how to narrow down the culprit. You have gigabit internet and your wired-in PC is only getting 90 Mbps, so is that outdated Ethernet cable getting in the way? While avoids Wi-Fi interference and can lower latency, plugging in a cable doesn't automatically mean you'll get ultra-fast speeds. Even if your internet service is speedy, a slow Ethernet connection can slow down file transfers between computers at home. won't provide a definitive answer, as it measures more than just the cable. The first place to start is to check the Ethernet link speed, and you don't need to purchase a tester to do this. field. Another method involves a shortcut that also works on Windows 10: press , right-click your Ethernet adapter and select . The negotiated connection rate is displayed in the (or your USB Ethernet adapter), then go to , as manually setting a speed may result in connection issues. There's a difference between seeing 1 Gbps here and actually downloading at 1 Gbps. The figure describes the connection between your computer and . It doesn't tell you your internet speed or the highest speed the cable can handle. The link-speed reading alone also can't confirm whether the cable is faulty. While you're looking into this, take a look at the lettering on the jacket of the cable. Markings like Cat5, Cat5e or Cat6 are typically found there, as the connectors are virtually identical and don't tell you much. Both Cat5e and Cat6 support gigabit Ethernet, so Cat6 is more than sufficient for 1,000 Mbps. The category isn't an absolute speed ceiling either. Older cables can sometimes support very high speeds for short runs , but a successful test doesn't mean they will perform the same way for longer runs. How to tell if your Ethernet cable is actually the problem If your computer reports 100 Mbps cable speeds when you expect 1 Gbps, verify the hardware on both ends. A 100 Mbps LAN port on a router, or a similarly limited USB Ethernet adapter, will limit the connection no matter . Even with gigabit-capable ports at both ends, a damaged wire or loose connector can still disrupt the connection or fall back to slower connections. Gigabit Ethernet utilizes all four twisted pairs of wires inside the cable, whereas conventional 100 Mbps Ethernet uses two. Start by reseating the connectors, then swap in a short, known-good cable using the same ports. If the reading changes from 100 Mbps to 1 Gbps, the original cable or its connectors are strong suspects for what's wrong. If nothing changes, check the port specifications and adapter settings before spending money on a replacement. to measure real throughput between two wired computers without involving your ISP. After installing it on both computers, turn off Wi-Fi, run on the other (replacing SERVER_IP with the local IP address of the first computer). Compare the results after swapping cables, keeping the rest of the setup the same. A multimeter or simple cable tester can determine some wiring faults, but neither can determine the maximum data rate that a cable supports. That requires specialized cable qualification equipment. Certification testers verify compliance with cabling standards.

articles.title: More than Just Storage: 8 Ways To Repurpose Your Old USB Flash Drive
articles.desc: It's time to do something with that drawer full of old USB flash drives. Breathe new life into unused tech with simple, useful tricks spanning an array of uses.
articles.content: More Than Just Storage: 8 Ways To Repurpose Your Old USB Flash Drive More than Just Storage: 8 Ways To Repurpose Your Old USB Flash Drive Smart ways to turn forgotten storage into something useful Remember the days when USB flash drives were the greatest thing since CD-ROMs? Those were obviously many days ago, but when thumb drives hit the shelves of, um, RadioShack, they pretty revolutionary. Saving and sharing files for school or work became significantly easier than file sharing with floppy disks — as long as your files weren't too big. But eventually those stick drives got bigger. 1GB, 4GB, 10GB. They got so big they became external hard drives. And then the equivalent of an extinction event for flash drives hit. The cloud was born, and it was endless. Now we could upload unlimited docs, photos and videos of any size to the ether for pretty cheap. Predictably, USBs went the way of Maxwell floppy discs. Post-cloud, most of our USB drives ended up in boxes and desk drawers next to our iPods, firewires and dial-up modems. However, unlike much of our museum-ready tech, you can actually use your old flash drives and portable hard drives for some pretty neat projects. They may even save you money and earn you a little more privacy. Make Yourself a NAS (Network Attached Storage) Device At some point in the past few years, Sonos, the wireless home audio system, stopped allowing users to point their speakers to music folders on their computers and external hard drives. Instead, Sonos users now had to share their music folder over their local network. This didn't mean you couldn't keep your library on the same old hard drive anymore. It simply meant your hard drive was functioning more like a Network Attached Storage (NAS) device, because the library was served over your network. The only downside was your computer had to be on to play your music. Normally, NAS drives don't have to be. But the idea itself sparked a few ideas. Imagine if you plugged that same old hard drive directly into your router. As long as your family was on the same network, it would now show up on everyone's devices. You could share whatever you wanted this way. Pics, recipes, to-do lists, books, movies — anything really. It would be like your private family cloud. No need to imagine, actually. It's very easy to set up. Here's how. Plug your external drive into your router's USB port, if you have one. Fire up your browser and open up your router settings. Check that file sharing is on. That's basically it. That drive should now show up on all your local devices like any other network volume or drive. If you're concerned about the steps you can take to improve online safety , as you should be, you can hand-pick the devices on your local area network (LAN) that can access your NAS. , is the network of devices that use your router to communicate with each other, which is important because only people on your network can access your files this way. Okay, so you've turned your beat-up Seagate into a functioning NAS device running off your router. Anyone on your network can access those files now. But let's say you want to share pics when you're somewhere else without direct access to your network. You can do that too, with a little more elbow grease. First, download and install the latest version (3.2.1 or later) of an application called HFS, short for "HTTP File Server," on your home computer. HFS works with Windows machines and Macs, and, best of all, it's free. In both cases, since you've already set up your NAS, your home computer should already recognize your USB device as a volume or drive. Copy the network path name or drag and drop the volume into your open HFS window. Now you're ready to share your files — with two important caveats. articles.title: Three Astrophysicists Ran 672 Scenarios for the Sun’s Death, and Most of the Larger-Burst Ones Ended Badly for the Outer Planets
articles.desc: The sun’s final act may not be the quiet exit scientists once pictured. Simulations point to a surprisingly turbulent ending for the giant planets, and the details are stranger than you’d expect.
articles.content: Three Astrophysicists Ran 672 Scenarios for the Sun’s Death, and Most of the Larger-Burst Ones Ended Badly for the Outer Planets New modeling suggests the outer planets may not survive the sun’s final act for nearly as long as scientists once believed. The timeline for their breakup shrinks from a quintillion years to roughly 1 billion For a long time, the standard picture held that would last for billions of years after the sun dies, until a passing star eventually disturbed them. The rock we live on will probably be long gone by then, but the giants might not make it either. That the fate of the solar system is tied to the sun is hardly a surprise. What changes is how the ending is expected to unfold: more violent, and a good deal faster. Theoretical astrophysicists Konstantin Batygin and Jim Fuller of the California Institute of Technology, together with Fred Adams of the University of Michigan, reached that conclusion in a paper in for billions of years before a passing star might upset it. The new work points instead to a quicker, more chaotic upheaval triggered by the dying sun itself. The key difference lies in how the sun loses its mass. Rather than treating the loss as smooth, the team considered the sun shedding its envelope in discrete bursts of stellar material. “Everything changes when the envelope departs in pieces,” the study authors wrote. To explore this, the researchers paired a detailed model of solar evolution with computer programs that follow changes in the orbits of the . They also checked whether the mass loss happened throughout the sun’s evolution into a Hundreds of Simulations, 3 Billion Years of Tracking , varying the burst sizes across them. For comparison, they also modeled cases in which the sun shed its mass smoothly. Each planetary system was then tracked for The study starts counting time when the star becomes a white dwarf, with t = 0 marking the end of its mass loss. But here’s the surprising part: even a planetary system that looks perfectly stable can fall apart billions of years later. articles.desc: The clean energy industry has learned the hard way that having the law on your side doesn’t always mean you win. This story was originally published by Grist. articles.content: The clean energy industry has learned the hard way that having the law on your side doesn’t always mean you win. This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist's weekly newsletter here. Since taking office for his second term, President Donald Trump has attempted to delay or cancel dozens of wind and solar projects. These projects all underwent extensive reviews to secure federal approval, but the Department of the Interior and other agencies have frozen their permits for vague “national security” reasons, or with no explanation at all. These attacks have all but tanked the offshore wind industry and have led many developers to take payouts from the administration rather than fight for permits. This attack is one big reason why solar and wind companies have been supportive of efforts in Congress to negotiate a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill. A group of senators reached a compromise earlier this month on a bill they call the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Lawmakers won’t vote on it until after the midterm elections, but the renewable energy sector has hailed it as a win. The bill would speed up environmental reviews for all kinds of energy projects, from transmission wires to oil pipelines, and it also contains a number of provisions that are designed to deter current and future presidents from blocking clean energy. Trump reportedly told aides just before the compromise became public that he would ease up on wind projects in order to reach a deal. Cracks are already emerging in the deal. While the renewable energy industry has remained steadfast in its support of the bill, a number of experts and key climate advocates are arguing that the “project certainty” provisions would do little to prevent Trump or another president from blocking solar farms and offshore wind turbines. The Trump administration itself threatened the compromise bill this week when it announced that it would review three permits for wind farms off the Atlantic Coast, including one that is already up and running. “The administration’s action against [the wind projects] just further demonstrates the lengths they will go to to obstruct clean energy progress, especially offshore wind,” said Elizabeth Klein, who led the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, which oversees offshore wind permits, under former president Joe Biden. The project certainty portion of the Senate bill has two key parts. First, it declares that the federal government “shall not take any new action that would revoke, rescind, withdraw, terminate, suspend, amend, or alter” a project that has already received a permit. This is just a forceful restatement of the status quo, since permits that are issued aren’t supposed to be canceled for no reason. But the bill goes further by offering companies two main remedies if the government does take such prohibited actions. One is the reinstatement of the permit — which is somewhat redundant. Judges have already shot down the Trump administration’s past attempts to stop wind projects, but the administration is still seeking to revoke those permits. If the bill passes, all the courts would be able to do is order it in stronger terms to restore them. The other remedy is a cash payout. The courts would be able to order the government to refund a project developer between 25 and 50 percent of the costs of their project, which for a big offshore wind farm could reach well into the billions. The money would come from the Judgment Fund, a bank account the federal government uses to pay out legal settlements. This fund typically disburses around $2 billion in settlements per year, and successful claims under the permitting bill could lead to a big spike in payouts. The other key part of project certainty in the bill is an anti-discrimination clause that would ban “disparate treatment” of any particular energy source, whether it’s solar panels or coal plants. If a wind developer found evidence that the government denied them permits as part of an anti-wind pattern, they could present that evidence to a judge. If persuaded, the judge would then order the government to restore the permit and pay the developer the entire construction cost of the wind farm — albeit only if the developer finished building it. Supporters of the bill argue that the promise of financial relief would help lure investors back to the renewable energy industry, which has been in turmoil under Trump. This is most important for offshore wind. Big companies like Ørsted and Equinor spent billions of dollars to build wind farms in the Atlantic under the Biden administration, but their costs ballooned after the pandemic snarled their supply chains and Trump tried to destroy their existing projects. These companies now view the United States as uninvestable, but Northeastern states still need a lot more offshore wind in order to meet their climate goals. The cash payout provision is supposed to help make the U.S. seem like a less risky place to invest. The American Clean Power Association, a trade group representing wind and solar developers, said in its analysis of the bill that “greater certainty lowers financing risk before construction and reduces the chance that years of development and investment will be stranded by a later policy reversal.” While the promise of reimbursement from the federal government would be good news for investors, it’s not clear that it would actually lead to more clean energy getting built. Opponents of the permitting reform bill point out that Trump has already been paying to stop renewable power plants from being built, albeit on a smaller scale. The president has worked out several deals to buy back offshore wind leases from energy developers in exchange for those developers committing to build a fossil fuel project elsewhere. These arrangements are being challenged in court, but in the meantime they function as repayments for leases that Trump intended to block. The project certainty “provisions are unlikely to deter the Trump Administration from continuing to mess with clean energy permits, since this administration has shown an eagerness to use the public’s money to advance its own policy goals,” said Matthew Littleton, a former attorney at the U.S. Department of Justice who worked on environmental law issues. Littleton also points out that the anti-discrimination provision may not work as intended. The baseline for calculating “disparate treatment” is the average pace of project approvals over the most recent five years. By the time Trump leaves office, he will have spent four years permitting oil and gas projects while delaying almost all major solar and wind efforts. This baseline would prevent wind developers from making a discrimination claim — while also preventing a future president from walking back support for new oil and gas. As if to highlight these risks, the White House has said in court filings over the past week that it is seeking to rescind permits for three offshore wind projects on the Atlantic Coast. One of these projects, the 700-megawatt Revolution Wind, is already complete and delivering power to Rhode Island, while the other two are still in the early stages. In each filing, the government has said only that it seeks to “reevaluate … compliance” with federal law. Over the past year, Democratic negotiators in the Senate have said that this sort of behavior would jeopardize any bipartisan deal. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, one of the authors of the bill, said in the spring that he would not endorse a compromise bill unless the administration stopped blocking wind farms. This week he appeared to change tack, and described the move against Revolution Wind as another reason to pass the bill. “Frankly, we need to get permitting certainty in law, and this proves it,” he said in a statement. The bill would in fact offer financial protection to a company like Ørsted, ensuring that a president could not wreck billions of dollars worth of investment with no justification at all. The question is whether it could end the government’s prejudicial assault against offshore wind. The answer could determine how millions of people in the Northeast keep their lights on and heat their homes, and right now, it’s up in the air. articles.content: TL;DR: US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $82.4 million in net outflows on October 16. BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for $71.8 million of withdrawals, with Fidelity’s FBTC recording about $10.6 million. BlackRock’s flagship spot Bitcoin ETF accounted for most of the selling as US-listed Bitcoin investment funds closed Friday’s session with net withdrawals of approximately $82.4 million. Farside Investors’ figures show that the iShares Bitcoin Trust, known as IBIT, lost $71.8 million on October 16. Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund recorded around $10.6 million in net outflows, while the remaining products were broadly flat on the day. That concentration matters because IBIT has become one of the clearest measures of Bitcoin demand through traditional brokerage accounts. Another Uneven Week For ETF Demand The latest withdrawals followed substantial redemptions earlier in the week. October 14 saw roughly $261 million leave the category, followed by a modest return to net inflows on October 15. Friday’s negative session therefore suggests demand remains unsettled rather than following a clear trend. Investors have seen considerably larger individual outflow days in the past. Earlier October withdrawals approached $485 million in a single session, demonstrating how rapidly demand through these products can shift. Context Is Important An ETF outflow is not a complete measure of institutional Bitcoin ownership, and it does not necessarily indicate that every underlying holder has abandoned a long-term position. Net inflows into the US spot Bitcoin ETF market since the products launched remained substantial despite the latest withdrawals. The next trading sessions will be important. A quick recovery would suggest another temporary adjustment, while continued redemptions from IBIT and FBTC would place greater emphasis on whether traditional investors are reducing their exposure amid broader market uncertainty. articles.title: Original iPhone OS 1 Lacked App Store, Copy and Paste and 3G
articles.desc: The original iPhone and iPhone OS 1 laid the foundation for modern smartphones but shipped without the App Store, copy and paste, 3G, GPS and MMS, features added in later releases.
articles.content: Original iPhone OS 1 Lacked App Store, Copy and Paste and 3G | Technology Pick countries on the world map and get breaking news alerts in your browser — free, no app. The original iPhone and iPhone OS 1 laid the foundation for modern smartphones but shipped without the App Store, copy and paste, 3G, GPS and MMS, features added in later releases. The original iPhone, running the software that would eventually be rebranded as iOS, launched without many of the features users now take for granted. iPhone OS 1 introduced the touch interface, pinch-to-zoom and double-tap gestures, and support for a proper mobile browser. marketed the device at the time as a widescreen iPod, and the handset reshaped the smartphone industry despite missing critical capabilities such as the , copy and paste, photo messaging and Home Screen wallpapers. The first-generation model also lacked 3G connectivity, which is why its successor was named the iPhone 3G. In the United States, AT&T was the exclusive carrier. The original iPhone had no built-in GPS, so Google Maps access was limited and offered no turn-by-turn directions. It also shipped without Touch ID or Face ID, the Retina Display, wireless charging, water resistance, or the Lightning and later USB-C connectors. Today it is hard to imagine an iPhone without hundreds of thousands of downloadable apps, but the original iPhone offered only pre-installed software. When the App Store was finally introduced, its software received over 10 million downloads by the first weekend of release. At that time, Apple said there were over 800 native apps available, with more than 200 free options, and more than 90 percent priced at less than $10. Copy and paste, a feature practically everyone uses today, was not available with iPhone OS 1. Users had to retype everything, and they could not even forward a friend's text to another person until OS 3.0. The original iPhone also lacked iMessage, which only became available in iOS 5, and Photo Messaging through the Multimedia Messaging Service was not supported either. MMS arrived later with iPhone OS 3.0 in 2009, but it was exclusive to the iPhone 3G and iPhone 3GS. Wallpapers were only released with iOS 4 in 2010, and before that users were left with a black wallpaper. In that department, Apple took a long time to catch up with its Android counterpart, though almost 20 years later the company offers several customizations for iPhone users. Siri was nowhere near being released with the first iPhone software. Siri was originally a standalone app developed for the iPhone, which Apple acquired to power its vision of a useful personal assistant. It was only included with new devices starting with the iPhone 4S, which ran iOS 5. Other features now considered basic were also unavailable, such as AirDrop, a functional Control Center, folders for apps, and the ability to delete and hide stock apps. Even iCloud, the most convenient way to back up data, was not available. In iPhone OS 2, Apple added MobileMe support, the predecessor of iCloud. For the longest time, users trying to keep their data safe relied on a wired connection between the iPhone and a computer through iTunes. That is no longer an option for iPhone users, as Apple ended support for iTunes on macOS in favor of separate Music, Podcasts and TV apps. Still, the first iPhone OS 1 created the foundation of the iPhone. While some features took longer to arrive, future releases eventually shaped what people expected from an iPhone. Video recording came with the iPhone 3GS, a selfie camera was introduced with the iPhone 4, bigger models arrived with the iPhone 6 and iPhone 6 Plus, and 5G support came with the iPhone 12. articles.content: Bentley May Be Owned By Volkswagen, But Its Cars Aren't Built In Germany | United States Pick countries on the world map and get breaking news alerts in your browser — free, no app. Under the hood it's VW Group tech, but the soul remains British. Inside Bentley's historic Crewe headquarters, where hand-stitched luxury lives on. A Bentley's blend of effortless pace and traditional craftsmanship is central to its unmistakable British character and charm. But is Bentley still truly British today? That's a fact enthusiasts still argue over, and those that say it isn't, point to a crucial moment in Bentley's history that happened almost 30 years ago. Bentley was founded in 1919, and made its name with a series of luxury, high-performance road cars, plus consecutive victories at races like Le Mans in the 1920s. But the Great Depression that followed the 1929 Wall Street Crash brought the brand to its knees, allowing rival Rolls-Royce to sweep in and take control. The Bentley name survived, but for the next six decades its cars would rely on Rolls-Royce chassis and engines. Some Rolls and Bentley cars were virtually identical during this period, although Bentley was still able to carve out its own identity with models like the By 1998, Rolls-Royce and Bentley's then-owner Vickers decided to put the brands up for sale. BMW was already supplying V12 engines, and it offered £340 million to take full control of Rolls-Royce and Bentley. It looked like a done deal. But another German automaker had plans of its own for the two British luxury brands. Volkswagen launched a £430 million offer, outbidding BMW for the Crewe factory in northwest England, the brands' cars and Rolls-Royce's Spirit of Ecstasy mascot and iconic Parthenon grille. But BMW had sneakily inked a deal with Rolls-Royce PLC, the aero engine business, to license the Rolls-Royce name for a pitiful £40 million . The two German giants eventually agreed to split the spoils: BMW would take Rolls-Royce and set up a brand-new factory at Goodwood, while Volkswagen would run Bentley from the old Rolls-Royce and Bentley base at Crewe. Retaining the Pyms Lane base, rather than relocating Bentley to Germany, helped maintain a connection between old and new Bentley eras. And every current Bentley from the Bentayga SUV to the, rolls out of the English plant. But that wasn't always the case. Demand for the Flying Spur was so strong after its 2005 launch, and again in 2013, that Bentley was forced to build a small number at VW's Dresden factory in Germany to keep up with orders. You'll still find plenty of German DNA in today's Bentleys. The Bentayga shares its platform with VW Group cousins like the Porsche Cayenne, and the Continental GT and Flying Spur share their architecture with the Porsche Panamera. The band's, a lovable relic from the Rolls-Royce days, died in 2020, and the current 3.0-liter V6 and 4.0-liter V8 engines are lifted from the VW parts bin, and cast in mainland Europe. Body shells are also imported from Germany, some having previously been made in Slovakia. But as the old saying goes, a car is more than the sum of its parts. The paint finish, trimming, and Mulliner personalization touches applied to new Bentleys, is the stuff that makes a modern Bentley so recognizable. Thanks to a massive £350 million overhaul, Crewe gained a state-of-the-art paint shop, new engineering technical center and a brand-new production line for the Torcal , the brand's first ever EV. Bentley has operated under Audi's control as part of VW's Progressive division since 2021, but it looks like it has no plans to relinquish its British roots any time soon. articles.title: AI is changing the way we understand human health
articles.desc: This article is authored by Ravi Gupta, vice president, Bioinformatics, MedGenome Labs Ltd.
articles.content: AI is changing the way we understand human health | Hindustan Times Copyright © HT Digital Streams Ltd. All rights reserved. AI is changing the way we understand human health This article is authored by Ravi Gupta, vice president, Bioinformatics, MedGenome Labs Ltd. Advances in science are giving us an increasingly detailed understanding of the human body. Today, we can sequence DNA, analyse tissue at a molecular level, interpret medical images, and continuously monitor vital signs, all of which is changing how diseases are diagnosed, treatments are developed, and care is delivered. But the paradox at the heart of this progress is that our ability to generate biological data is outpacing our ability to interpret and translate that data into meaningful insights. India faces an especially significant challenge. The country has roughly 64 doctors per 100,000 people, compared with a global average of nearly 150. With around 70% of the population living in rural areas and only an estimated 20,000–22,000 radiologists serving a population of 1.4 billion, the gap in access and capacity is significant. Meanwhile, global imaging volumes are growing by around 5% annually, as genomic and multi-omics technologies generate biological data at unprecedented scale and complexity. The challenge, therefore, lies not in generating this data, but in processing, connecting and interpreting it quickly and efficiently enough to turn it into meaningful, actionable clinical insights. As the volume and complexity of health data continue to grow, executing this at scale is becoming increasingly challenging. A pathology test can reveal cellular changes, a genomic test can uncover thousands of genetic variants, and a medical scan can reveal subtle patterns, that may be difficult to distinguish from noise. In some cases, a patient’s risk only becomes apparent when insights from these biological data are considered together. Computational biology, the use of statistics and algorithms to analyse and interpret biological data, offers a way to work through this complexity by analysing datasets and identifying relationships that would be difficult to process manually, helping translate this complex data into more meaningful clinical insights. However, conventional approaches can be time-consuming and prone to error due to manual processing, particularly when working with large, complex and heterogeneous datasets. The limited availability of specialists in every field further constrains the ability to cater to the growing volume of biological data efficiently. The growing need for faster, more accurate and scalable health care has created an opportunity for emerging technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learning to complement computational biology and enable faster, and efficient analysis. Today, AI models are being integrated into computational biology where specialist expertise is limited or unevenly distributed, AI can be used to support high-volume preliminary analysis and flag cases that require closer clinical review. AI models can augment the analysis of medical images, genomic sequences and multi-omics data helping scientists and clinicians to detect abnormalities, classify disease, estimate risk and support biological discovery. In Indian multi-site studies, automated reporting with human verification has nearly halved radiology turnaround times demonstrating how technology can strengthen clinical expertise and improve efficiency. AI-based tools are being used to support interpretation of chest X-rays and detect early signs of vision-threatening retinal abnormalities. articles.content: Ward 2 City Council Candidate Rolf Arands | News | gillettenewsrecord.com You have permission to edit this article. : Now retired; chemical engineering and advanced research for 16 years; software engineering and technical/risk analyst for 14 years; physical therapist assistant for 9 years. According to the Insurance Services Office, Gillette is currently understaffed in terms of fire protection for a city of its size. A joint plan to increase personnel collapsed earlier this year. As a member of the city council, what steps would you take to see the department properly funded? As a citizen, I was present at both commissioner and council meetings when staffing of fire fighting was discussed between both boards. The city ranked fire and police the No. 1 priority for funding on Resolution 2830. For city and county, ensuring the safety of the firefighters and the community is paramount. As councilman, I will work closely as a partner with the commissioners to ensure full funding. For the city, this may mean examination and delaying other projects to ensure funding. Additionally, we need to ensure salaries are competitive to retain staff. Finally, we need to fully utilize state-level support for our firefighters. I have testified before the state’s appropriations committee on funding firefighting and believe there is considerable state-level support available. Over the past few years, utility prices have greatly increased across Wyoming, leading to pushback from some in the community. In what ways can the city council work to combat rising utility prices? What strategies would you propose if elected? In examining city budgets, utility-related projects and spending, there has been considerable use of debt for utility projects. At the end of FY2025, the city had about $97 million in utility-related debt. There have been numerous rate increases to service debt, especially for wastewater. These rate increases have far exceeded inflation in some cases. There has been recent discussion of future rate increases to service debt. City staff have discussed plans to incur more debt in the near future. Interest rates are rising which will increase debt servicing costs. Long-term budgeting must minimize or eliminate this reliance on costly debt. There are cost-cutting measures that I’ve presented in forums and on Facebook such as optimizing city irrigation and diverting heavy cardboard out of the waste stream. articles.desc: Astronomers using the Japan-led XRISM satellite have successfully tracked plasma flowing onto a neutron star for the first time.
articles.content: Giant 'farting' star 13,000 light-years away triggers record X-ray flares - Space News - News - Daily Express US The tiny neutron star, GX 301-2, orbits right through this chaotic mess A massive "farting" star located 13,000 light-years from Earth is releasing gassy bursts and triggering powerful X-ray flares from a neighboring celestial body. scientists utilized an advanced X-ray imaging and spectroscopy instrument to measure enormous quantities of gas streaming from named Wray 997 onto its significantly smaller companion GX 301-2, producing a tremendous energy release never before documented anywhere in The cosmic phenomenon, currently occurring in the BP Crucis system, essentially functions like an enormous domino effect, whereby gas from the larger star triggers an outpouring of accumulated energy from a smaller neutron star, Saturn's moon Enceladus may support alien life, new study suggests Youngest 'alien planet' ever found is 5,000 times younger than Earth Astronomers writing in Science Advances theorized that the neutron star passes through a concentrated stream of gas from Wray 977 and captures some of it. The more intense flares occur closer to the giant star, where the stream is more concentrated. Scientists monitored the system for approximately 16 hours, near the conclusion of a strong flare. Variations in its X-ray spectrum revealed gas traveling toward the neutron star at roughly 335,000mph, about 500 times the speed of sound. The gas isn't just floating over; it is being pulled down at an astonishing 335,000 mph Wray 977, believed to be approximately 60 times larger than the Sun and 40 times heavier, derives its remarkable brightness from its constant, fart-like flow of ionized gas, referred to by scientists as a "stellar wind." Although these fart-like flares were only recently recorded — because the stars involved are 13,000 light-years from Earth — they actually occurred approximately 13 millennia ago. Commenting on the extraordinary findings, NASA researcher Roi Rahin noted that they would enable scientists to test their understanding of how such processes unfold in the universe "in much greater detail" than ever before. He stated: "We've never before seen clear indications of wind plasma falling onto a compact object. We can now test our understanding of these processes in much greater detail."
